subject: Career
title: Why Rejection Isn't Always About You
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Rejection Isn't Always About You usable.

hook.text: You nailed the interview. You got rejected. Before spiraling, consider: it might not be about you.

buildup.text: Internal candidates, budget freezes, and reorganizations kill roles after interviews happen.

discovery.text: Attribution error makes us assume personal failure when systemic factors are often the cause.

twist.text: Companies sometimes interview for roles they've already internally filled. It happens more than you think.

climax.text: Always ask for feedback. Even a brief response helps you separate skill gaps from bad luck.

punchline.text: Rejection is data, not a verdict on your worth.

quiz.question: What cognitive error makes us over-personalize interview rejection?

details.summary: Interview rejections frequently result from factors entirely outside the candidate's control, including internal candidates, budget freezes, shifting role requirements, and interviewer biases. Personalizing every rejection distorts your self-assessment.
details.whyItMatters: Candidates who internalize every rejection develop learned helplessness that sabotages future interviews. Understanding systemic factors preserves confidence for the next opportunity.
takeaways: Up to fifty percent of rejections involve factors you cannot influence
Request specific feedback to distinguish personal gaps from external causes
Track your rejection patterns to identify genuine improvement areas

faq.question: How can you get useful feedback after being rejected from a job interview?
faq.answer: Send a gracious email thanking them and specifically asking for one or two areas where you could improve. Many recruiters will share feedback when asked politely and specifically. Generic requests for feedback are less likely to receive a response.

faq.question: How many rejections are normal before landing a job in a competitive market?
faq.answer: In competitive fields, receiving ten to twenty rejections per offer is common at senior levels. At entry level, the ratio can be even higher. Treating job searching as a numbers game rather than a referendum on your worth reduces emotional toll.
